Peter combines a model with your current R workspace. A language model requests tools and
returns a session; a decision model returns a typed vector. The same `peter()` gateway handles
both. An inline agent can compute on a multi-GB object already loaded in R, keep intermediate
variables, and reuse them across turns. This guide explains where that computation happens,
what the model receives, and where memory or file transfers still occur.

## One language model turn

1. `peter()` captures the prompt and context expressions and selects the model and permission mode.
2. It describes the workspace and attached objects within a token budget, then builds the request.
3. The provider streams a reply. Each gptr tool request passes through the permission gate.
4. R code runs in the selected environment; file and external tools use their own documented paths.
5. Tool results return to the model until it finishes, is interrupted, or reaches a limit.
6. The session retains the conversation, status, usage and a designated result, if there is one.

This example uses a scripted provider, so it runs offline and always requests the same R code:


``` r
library(gptr)
work = new.env()
work$d = mtcars
fake = gptr_fake_provider(list(
  list(tool = "r", input = list(code = "fit = lm(mpg ~ wt, data = d)\ngptr_return(fit)")),
  "The regression is ready."
))
s = peter("Fit fuel economy against weight.", d = work$d, model = fake,
          envir = work, mode = "auto")
s$text
#> [1] "The regression is ready."
s$status
#> [1] "idle"
coef(s$value)
#> (Intercept)          wt
#>   37.285126   -5.344472
```

`gptr_return(fit)` designates `fit` as the result. The final model text is `s$text`; it does
not automatically become the fitted object. The result also remains available as `work$fit`.

## Where objects live

The default `envir` is the calling frame. At the console that is usually the global workspace;
inside a function it is that function's frame. Supply an environment when you want the work to
persist in a particular place. Named context such as `d = work$d` labels an attachment;
it does not create a binding called `d` in a different evaluation environment.


``` r
gptr_describe(work$d, budget = 60)
#> [1] "<data.frame> 32 x 11, 7 KB"
#> [2] "  mpg:dbl cyl:dbl disp:dbl hp:dbl drat:dbl wt:dbl qsec:dbl vs:dbl am:dbl gear:dbl carb:dbl"
ls(work)
#> [1] "d"   "fit"
identical(s$value, work$fit)
#> [1] TRUE
```

The inline `r` tool evaluates against those actual bindings. It does not need to write a
dataset to a file or reload it before the next tool call. Attach a large object as a plain name
visible in that environment; gptr captures that name without retaining another copy of the
object in the conversation. An expression such as `subset(d, ...)` still performs ordinary R
work when evaluated, and may allocate a new object.

Workspace context lists names, classes, shapes and sizes within a budget. Attached objects get
compact descriptions that can include schema, sample values and summaries. The full local
object remains available to R code. Printed tool output is bounded, with an output handle for
long results, and captured plots can be sent as images. Those previews and results may contain
data values; the permission and egress controls still apply. System 1 decisions instead send
encoded input states under their own size rules; see [System 1](system-one.html).

`context = "names"` reduces workspace context to names and attachments to headers;
`context = "none"` omits both built-in workspace and attached-object descriptions. These settings
leave R objects available to the tools and do not suppress prompt text, tool results or every
other context block. See [Configuration](configuration.html) and
[Token efficiency](token-efficiency.html).

Ordinary R copy-on-modify rules still apply. Modifying an object, keeping aliases, fitting a
model or calling a package can allocate substantial memory. Checkpoints retain supported
pre-images for undo, and workers, bridges and artifact snapshots have their own transfer or
copy costs. An overlay lets reads find the parent object's binding while keeping ordinary
assignments local; it does not isolate changes to reference objects or external resources.

A continued session reuses its kept home environment unless you explicitly supply a new `envir`.
When the default environment is a function call frame, gptr uses it during the active run and
does not retain it as the session's home afterward. An explicit working environment can retain
named results.
An explicit `gptr_fork(s)` branches the conversation and uses a workspace overlay. Restoring a
session from disk restores its conversation; it does not restore all of your R objects.

Each model request has provider and transport latency. R evaluation takes the time and memory
its code needs; memory pressure can slow work or make an allocation fail. A file-backed matrix,
Arrow dataset or database connection may read from disk through its package even when its R
handle is already loaded. Use those packages' normal subset and compute operations rather
than assuming every object is a fully resident data frame.

## What the session retains


``` r
s$id
#> [1] "sb95b5c3e33"
s$model
#> [1] "fake/fake-1"
s$turns
#> [1] 1
names(s$messages[[1]])
#> [1] "role"      "content"   "source"    "timestamp"
gptr_usage(s)
#>   group        requests  input  output  cache_read  cache_write  cost
#> 1 sb95b5c3e33  2         3241   20      0           0            0
#>
#> # 1 row
#> 2 requests, 3.2k tokens in, $0.0000
identical(gptr_last(), s)
#> [1] TRUE
```

| Interface | Use |
|---|---|
| `s$text`, `s$value`, `s$status` | Inspect the latest answer, designated R result and state |
| `s$messages`, `s$history`, `s$usage` | Inspect conversation, the per-message history table and accounting |
| `s |> peter("next question")` | Add a turn to the same conversation |
| `gptr_step()`, `gptr_wait()`, `gptr_steer()`, `gptr_cancel()` | Drive or control a session |
| `gptr_sessions()`, `gptr_resume()`, `gptr_last()` | Find stored or live sessions |
| `gptr_on()` | Attach a session event handler |
| `gptr_fork()`, `gptr_checkpoints()`, `gptr_rewind()` | Branch or recover supported state |

Printing `s$history` or `summary(s)` shows eight recent messages and session details, without
a model request. The underlying table keeps every message; unknown token counts stay unknown.


``` r
s$history
#>   turn  role         preview                   tools  tokens
#> 1 1     user         Fit fuel economy agai...         8
#> 2 1     assistant                              r      1632
#> 3 1     tool_result  + fit <lm length 12>      r      5
#> 4 1     assistant    The regression is ready.         1629
#> # 4 recorded messages
#> idle . fake/fake-1 . 1 turn . 3.3k tokens . $0.0000 . sb95b5c3e33
print(s$history, n = Inf)
#>   turn  role         preview                   tools  tokens
#> 1 1     user         Fit fuel economy agai...         8
#> 2 1     assistant                              r      1632
#> 3 1     tool_result  + fit <lm length 12>      r      5
#> 4 1     assistant    The regression is ready.         1629
#> # 4 recorded messages
#> idle . fake/fake-1 . 1 turn . 3.3k tokens . $0.0000 . sb95b5c3e33
as.data.frame(s$history)
#>   turn        role                          preview tools tokens
#> 1    1        user Fit fuel economy against weight.            8
#> 2    1   assistant                                      r   1632
#> 3    1 tool_result             + fit <lm length 12>     r      5
#> 4    1   assistant         The regression is ready.         1629
```

Without an initialized project workspace, session files use a temporary directory.
`gptr_init()` creates `.gptr/` for project storage. Recording an R document is a separate choice;
see [Script as history](script-as-history.html).

A history document records executed code, decisions and bounded output. It does not
automatically archive the full input dataset. Replay runs the recorded R procedure again;
provide its input objects, packages and required files in a fresh session. Answer caches,
checkpoints and artifact data snapshots are separate storage mechanisms.

## Permissions and concurrency

`manual` is the default: actions classified as read-only can run, while changes require approval.
`plan` is for inspection and proposals; `edits` allows approved classes of project file edits;
`auto` allows ordinary tool work without prompting. Critical, secret and control guards remain
separate. A permission gate is not an isolation boundary. External CLIs also have their own sandbox
and tool controls; live R requests still pass through gptr's MCP gate. Use [Configuration](configuration.html)
and `?gptr_security` to choose a mode and understand its limits.

HTTP requests, CLI processes, MCP connections and workers share a cooperative reactor.
Multiple requests can wait for I/O together. Inline R code runs serially in the owning R process
and pauses its reactor callbacks until evaluation returns. A worker is a separate R process and receives
serializable context; it does not share the parent workspace. See
[Teams and background work](teams-and-background.html).
